title: Reform UK reporting Green leader Zack Polanski to police over Instagram post
description: Reform UK have reported Green Party leader Zack Polanski to the police, after he shared an Instagram post including a photo of a man wearing a top fea
body: Reform UK have reported Green Party leader Zack Polanski to the police, after he shared an Instagram post including a photo of a man wearing a top featuring the name "Nigel" alongside an image of a guillotine.One of several images showed a man in a black t-shirt with a large guillotine below the words "We're only making plans for Nigel".Sharing a screenshot on X, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "If I was to post anything as inciteful then I would expect to be arrested, and so should Polanski."A Green Party spokesperson said: "Once this image was brought to [Zack's] attention he immediately unshared the post. He unequivocally does not support this type of dangerous message."Polanski had shared the photo with his 713,000 followers in a post containing several pictures of a Green Party event on Sunday, having accepted a request to collaborate with another account.In a post on X, the Metropolitan Police said: "We received a third-party report relating to an image shared on social media. We take reports of this nature extremely seriously, and officers are conducting enquiries into the matter."The words "We're only making plans for Nigel" are the same as the lyrics of a 1979 song by band XTC, external.The Green Party spokesperson said: "Zack condemns the image on the T-shirt. He was tagged in a post with 20 images and clicked accept without realising there was more to it than he had seen."The T-shirt is clearly in poor taste, especially at a time of heightened fears for the security of public figures, having experienced multiple threats himself."He and the Green Party call on everyone involved in public discourse to show kindness and not encourage more division."The BBC understands Polanski has not been contacted by police.A photographer with the username just.barold claimed responsibility, external for the photo, which he said was of someone wearing a satirical T-shirt, and apologised to Polanski on X, saying "this is not his fault" and adding he had reported himself to the police.In a series of posts, the freelance photographer said: "This wasn't intended to offend anyone and it's clearly not intended as a serious threat to anyone's safety whatsoever."They added: "This performative outrage is just that, and if people want to come and take it out on someone then take it out on the person who took the picture, and who then posted it."However, Reform's home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf said the image showed "a photo of man calling for the beheading of Nigel Farage", which he claimed could be an "incitement to murder".Yusuf confirmed Reform UK had reported the post to police and will also report Polanski to to the monitoring officer at the Greater London Assembly, where the Green leader is an elected member."To do this just two weeks after our friend Ann was murdered is staggering," Yusuf said. "This is incitement to murder. It should be treated as such by the police."Prominent Reform member Widdecombe, 78, was found dead in her home in Haytor, Devon, on 9 July. A man, 28, has been charged with her murder. Her death reignited a row about the security of political figures in public life, with this year marking the 10th anniversary of the murder of Labour MP Jo Cox and the fifth anniversary of the murder of Conservative MP David Amess.Following Widdecombe's death, Polanski called for all party leaders to get extra security.Asked about Widdecombe's death at the time, he told BBC Breakfast: "I am worried and I have been worried for a long time."I would encourage the government to provide me with extra security, but that is a choice for them."Andy Burnham also backed a serious review of MPs' security earlier this month.Reform UK's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick had accused the government of a "dereliction of duty" over Farage's security, after it emerged the party turned down a government-funded security offer last year.The Home Office said Jenrick's comments were "categorically untrue", and that independent security experts, not ministers, held responsibility for deciding MPs' security.

schema.headline: Reform UK reporting Green leader Zack Polanski to police over Instagram post

title: The Odyssey: Millions see leaked copy of movie on X
description: "The whole Odyssey film in an embedded video on Twitter. Crazy," wrote someone in a post on X."Someone leaked The Odyssey movie in HD. I thought it wa
body: "The whole Odyssey film in an embedded video on Twitter. Crazy," wrote someone in a post on X."Someone leaked The Odyssey movie in HD. I thought it was fake but it's true," said another user.The Hollywood Reporter said, external a lower-quality version appeared on X on Sunday, and was removed two hours later after amassing almost 50,000 views.In response, film studio Universal said: "We became aware of the unauthorised posting of the film and immediately initiated takedown protocols."We take copyright infringement seriously and will pursue all appropriate remedies to protect our content and intellectual property rights."The leak is unlikely to do significant harm to the film's box office performance - it earned $215m (£160m) around the world in its second weekend, taking its total to $640m (£480m).

schema.headline: The Odyssey: Millions see leaked copy of movie on X

title: Bill Oddie: Comedian who found nature a welcome refuge from mental illness
description: Image source, Getty ImagesBySam WoodhouseBill Oddie, who has died at the age of 85, was one of Britain's best known comedians and naturalists.A produc
body: Image source, Getty ImagesBySam WoodhouseBill Oddie, who has died at the age of 85, was one of Britain's best known comedians and naturalists.A product of the Cambridge Footlights, the cradle of so much post-war British comedy, he shot to fame in the 1970s as a member of the anarchic Goodies.Bird watching was a lifelong passion and he moved into presenting nature programmes, including the BBC's Springwatch.But his life was plagued by bouts of acute depression which caused repeated admissions to psychiatric hospitals - where Oddie suffered from severe lithium poisoning as a result of his treatment.Image caption, A beardless Bill Oddie (R) with the cast of I'm Sorry I'll Read That Again in 1965William Edgar Oddie was born near Rochdale, Lancashire on 7 July 1941.His ancestors on both sides were mill workers. However, his father Harry had made good, moved to Birmingham and worked as an accountant at the Midlands Electricity Board.The comedian later said his father's work ethic greatly influenced his approach to his own career. But Bill saw little of his mother Lillian during his childhood.She had been diagnosed with schizophrenia and spent much of her time in hospital. Oddie later discovered that her depression had followed the premature deaths of his two older siblings.Image source, Radio Times via Getty ImagesImage caption, Future Goodies Bill Oddie and Graeme Garden photographed in 1973As a child, he became interested in bird watching - a record of one of his first observations was even preserved in a West Midlands Bird Club publication in 1956.After leaving King Edward's School, where he was an enthusiastic rugby player, he went to Pembroke College, Cambridge to read English.There he became involved with the Footlights Club, which numbered Graeme Garden and Tim Brooke-Taylor among its members.Oddie wrote for and appeared in the famous 1964 review, A Clump of Plinths, which, having taken the Edinburgh Festival by storm, travelled to London's West End as well as New Zealand and the United States.Image source, Hulton Archive via Getty ImagesImage caption, The Goodies: (l to r) Graeme Garden, Tim Brooke-Taylor and Bill Oddie in 1975While still at Cambridge, Oddie wrote material for David Frost's satirical BBC TV show That Was the Week That Was. He fondly recalled a poem he wrote for fellow comedian Lance Percival in the style of The Ballad of Eskimo Nell about Camberley Kate who seduced dustbin men in Kent.Having left university, he went on to join the cast of the BBC radio show I'm Sorry I'll Read That Again, which featured many of the Footlights performers.He was also developing as a composer, writing many of the show's songs, some of which appeared on an album Distinctly Oddie in 1967.Image caption, The Goodies on their "trandem"While some of the old Footlights team went off to form Monty Python, Oddie -  together with Graeme Garden and Tim Brooke-Taylor - created The Goodies.It featured three characters on their "trandem" who pedalled about offering themselves for hire with the tagline "We Do Anything, Anywhere, Anytime".This spawned a series of comical situations, much slapstick and the use of fairly primitive special effects, mainly sped-up film.One of the memorable episodes was Kitten Kong, in which a giant feline toppled the Post Office Tower. A version of this episode won the Silver Rose at Montreux TV Festival in 1972.Oddie composed a number of comic songs for the series, often parodies of contemporary pop music. The most successful, Funky Gibbon, reached number four in the UK charts and the trio performed it on Top of the Pops.Forty years later, the track was re-released and the profits given to a campaign to preserve the primate's habitat.Image caption, Bill Oddie helped birdwatching find new audiencesThe Goodies ran on BBC Television for most of the 1970s, eventually transferring to ITV for a short - and less than successful - period.The show became cult viewing in Australia - and the team reformed to tour the country in 2005 - but the BBC never repeated it in the UK, something that annoyed the three performers.Garden eventually went on record to suggest that the lack of repeats was punishment for the trio's "disloyalty", saying in 2020: "It seems they've held that grudge ever since."Oddie and Garden also co-wrote the scripts for many of ITV's Doctor in the House comedy series. But Oddie's childhood interest in ornithology had never waned and, by the mid 1970s, he was developing a career as a naturalist.He made guest appearances on several programmes including Animal Magic. And the humorous style of his  Little Black Bird Book, published in 1980, made it a bestseller. "Bird-watchers are tense, competitive, selfish, shifty, dishonest, distrusting, boorish, pedantic, unsentimental, arrogant and - above all, envious" he wrote.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Bill Oddie hosted the BBC Springwatch programme until 2009It also heralded a flowering of his career as a TV presenter and he seemed to be rarely off our screens.The Great Bird Race, for Channel 4 in 1983, was followed by a number of programmes for the BBC including The Great Kenyan Bird Safari and Oddie in Paradise.In 1985, the BBC ran a 50-minute Nature Watch special: Bill Oddie - Bird Watcher, in which he travelled to many of the areas where he loved to watch birds.By the beginning of the new century, he was one of the BBC's best-loved presenters with shows like Birding with Bill Oddie and Bill Oddie Goes Wild, which took birdwatching to new audiences.Northumberland Wildlife Trust chief Mike Pratt paid tribute to Oddie's "influential" and entertaining presence as a naturalist, serving as the charity's patron for nearly 30 years. "Bill was a fantastic inspiration to my generation of young conservationists from the 1970s onwards," said Pratt. "He made being a naturalist fun and exciting, and led me and many of my counterparts into campaigning and taking action to save wildlife."We will miss his support for what he genuinely cared about - life in all its forms."Image caption, Simon King, Bill Oddie and Kate Humble on the BBC's Springwatch programmeIn 2004, Britain Goes Wild pulled in a record audience when it aired on BBC Two. A year later it returned as Springwatch, with Autumnwatch following a year later.When he wasn't fronting wildlife programmes, Oddie popped up on a string of quiz shows, had a part in a Doctor Who episode and, a memorable and poignant appearance in the BBC's genealogy series, Who Do You Think You Are?He also carved out a career as a voice-over artist. He was the cat in a Thompson Directory advert and made a series of spots for the DIY chain B&Q. He later described this aspect of his life as one of the most financially lucrative.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Bill Oddie campaigned against the illegal trade in ivoryHe lent his celebrity to the campaign against the illegal trade in ivory, warning that poachers kill thousands of elephants a year.But Oddie had always been prone to bouts of depression and he was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder - which he occasionally blamed on his remote relationship with his mother.Oddie parted company with Springwatch in 2008.The star told the Daily Mirror in 2018, external: "I never had a proper explanation."I was called in and told: 'We won't be asking you to make any more programmes.'"Oddie added: "Unfortunately, my bipolar element had come into it and I could be very tetchy."The Mirror reported that the BBC did not know at the time he had a conditon, but later issued a statement saying: "We wish Mr Oddie a speedy recovery."Image source, Future via Getty ImagesImage caption, Bill Oddie suffered severe lithium poisoning as a result of his mental health treatment"At the time I was flabbergasted, " he said in a 2015 interview, external with the Independent."But a year later, I was diagnosed as bipolar. I thought back. If I knew then what I know now, I'd have accepted that I was going through a manic phase."The audience missed him. Before he left, the show had averaged 3.19 million. After he left, that figure fell to 2.55 million.Oddie later revealed his condition caused him to try and take his own life.In 2020, he announced that he had been severely ill as a result of lithium poisoning: a treatment aimed at stabilising his moods.He later posted on social media that "the past few years have been grim for me. "Lost enthusiasm, but I am still here."His outside interests included music. He once did a spell as a radio DJ playing jazz and his house contained his collection of thousands of CDs.Oddie was also a passionate supporter of the Green Party and gave his time, and fame, to bolster wildlife charities such as the RSPB.His 1967 marriage to the musician, Jean Hart, ended in divorce. In 1983, he married Laura Beaumont, who had previously worked with him on a number of projects.Oddie was a true polymath, a man who seemed to make a success of everything to which he turned his hand. But it was his conservation work that gave him the most satisfaction. "Wildlife," he said, "has long been a refuge - probably more than I realise."

schema.headline: Bill Oddie: Comedian who found nature a welcome refuge from mental illness

title: 'Do the right thing': Savannah Guthrie pleads to mother's kidnappers
description: It was one of two ransom notes believed to be credible that were addressed to Nancy Guthrie's family and sent to news media shortly after her January
body: It was one of two ransom notes believed to be credible that were addressed to Nancy Guthrie's family and sent to news media shortly after her January kidnapping. The first demanded millions in Bitcoin for her release; the second stated that she had died, according to US media, which cited unnamed sources. Why the trail went cold in Nancy Guthrie caseIn her latest video posted on Monday, Savannah Guthrie addressed the possible kidnappers. "It has been months since our mum was taken from us," Guthrie said. "Our family is in agony. We are in a nightmare that will not end. Nothing about our situation has changed. We have done our part, and we will never stop looking for her. We will always ache for her and feel that hole in our hearts."She added: "Help us bring this situation to an end. For all of us, no matter where we've been and what we've done, I believe there is always a way home. Please make the right choice."The Pima County Sheriff's Department has not commented on the contents of any apparent ransom notes, but the department said their investigation "remains active and ongoing".The BBC's US partner, CBS News, and other news outlets reported that law enforcement had requested that media hold off publishing details of any of the notes while they investigated Nancy Guthrie's disappearance.The FBI and Pima County have spent months investigating her mysterious abduction from her Arizona home. Nancy Guthrie, who needs daily medication, vanished sometime after she was dropped off at her home by relatives on the January evening almost six months ago. She failed to show up the following morning at a friend's house to watch a virtual Sunday church service.Earlier this year, authorities released images of a masked and armed suspect who covered the  front door camera at Nancy Guthrie's home before her disappearance. An initial ransom note was sent the day after she went missing and demanded millions in Bitcoin for her release.It gave specific details about her home, as well as details about her bedroom and the home's surroundings, investigators told CBS.Savannah Guthrie has said some ransom notes sent to the family were believed to be fake. She has said that her mother may no longer be alive.

schema.headline: 'Do the right thing': Savannah Guthrie pleads to mother's kidnappers

title: New technical education routes to be offered at 14 in England
description: Pupils will be able to study subjects like manufacturing and AI alongside core academic learning from age 14 under new government plans for education
body: Pupils will be able to study subjects like manufacturing and AI alongside core academic learning from age 14 under new government plans for education in England.The government said the courses available from Year 10 would be linked to local jobs and industries.The announcement comes after data published earlier this year showed more than one million young people across the UK were not in education, employment or training, or "Neet" - the highest level in more than 12 years.School leaders' unions welcomed the government's ambition to improve technical education, but called for greater clarity on how and when the changes would be implemented, and how they would be paid for.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said "for too long" students had been told to take academic subjects to "do well and be respected"."My message to young people is this - whether you choose construction, coding or classics, or maths, manufacturing or mechanics, you'll get the skills you need and be given the respect you deserve," he said.He said the government was delivering the "major shake-up" required to fix the youth unemployment crisis in Britain, starting with improving the availability and quality of technical education.This would provide students with skills training, work experience and connections with employers, the government said.It said students would have the chance to combine core academic subjects such as English and maths with a high-quality technical education linked to the jobs available in their area. "They will be able to spend time with employers and gain real-world experience," it said.The BBC understands that the government expects the new pathways into work to be up and running in some areas by 2028.The plans for technical education reform will build on local initiatives like the MBacc, or Greater Manchester Baccalaureate, which was announced in 2023 by the now prime minister when he was the city's mayor.Launched there in September 2024, it has provided a framework for pupils to pick GCSE subjects in both academic and technical subjects which align with growing local industries, like green energy or digital.The government said it would be working with regional mayors, local leaders, schools, colleges and employers to deliver its plans nationally.Education Secretary Lucy Powell said the announcement "marks the start of a real shared effort with employers, businesses, mayors and councils to design an education system that connects young people to jobs and careers in their local area"."The technological revolution we are living through should mean young people become the fresh lifeblood our economy needs to adapt and grow," she said."I want to make sure this generation is able to seize that opportunity, whatever their background or postcode."Milburn said the changes announced for England on Tuesday were "very welcome"."They are a big step in the right direction and consistent with the findings of my review," he said."A whole system reset is needed across health, welfare and labour market policy as well as in education and skills. "I know the PM recognises this and my final report will outline the further changes that are needed."But Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary, said the announcements "don't come anywhere close to undoing the damage Labour has already done to the job market". "We all want to see better opportunities for young people and a boost to technical education, but this announcement is all over the place... "It's not clear whether or not Labour intends to replace GCSEs, which would be a disaster. "The focus should be on the knowledge-rich curriculum that has helped the most deprived children."Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said he was pleased the government was treating the "shocking" number of Neets as an "urgent priority".Though he said the union supported its aims, he said there was "little detail" about what the plans for educational reform would look like in practice.He added that it was "wrong" to make major educational policy announcements in the middle of the school summer holiday.Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT), said school leaders "support the principle of giving technical and vocational education the same status and recognition as more traditional academic routes"."However, this announcement sets out a direction of travel rather than detailed proposals, and schools will need much greater clarity about what it means in practice and over funding," he added.

schema.headline: New technical education routes to be offered at 14 in England

title: John Stones: England defender in advanced talks to join Inter Milan
description: England defender John Stones is in advanced talks with Inter Milan about joining the Italian side on a free transfer.The centre-half is a free agent a
body: England defender John Stones is in advanced talks with Inter Milan about joining the Italian side on a free transfer.The centre-half is a free agent after leaving Manchester City at the end of June.Stones has been the subject of major interest from clubs across Europe, including Chelsea and Juventus.But Serie A champions Inter have held positive discussions with the 32-year-old and are understood to be leading the race to sign the Premier League and Champions League winner on a two-year contract. Stones made 295 appearances for City after joining from Everton for £47.5m in 2016.He helped City win six Premier League titles, the Champions League, two FA Cups, five League Cups, three Community Shields, the Club World Cup and the Uefa Super Cup.The former Barnsley defender has won 93 international caps and was part of the England squad who finished third at the World Cup.

schema.headline: John Stones: England defender in advanced talks to join Inter Milan

title: Wildfire now nine miles from French city of Bordeaux, mayor warns
description: The mayor of Bordeaux has said he is bracing for "all eventualities", as one of multiple wildfires burning in France is now 15km (nine miles) from the
body: The mayor of Bordeaux has said he is bracing for "all eventualities", as one of multiple wildfires burning in France is now 15km (nine miles) from the south-western city."We are preparing to accommodate a large number of people should further evacuations be ordered," said Thomas Cazenave. President Emmanuel Macron, visiting the fire-ravaged area in the Gironde region, said the country was facing a "completely unprecedented wildfire" - the "toughest since World War Two".Some 220,000 people have been evacuated in France and more than 100,000 in Spain, where fires are burning "uncontrolled" west of Madrid.Another intense heatwave on Tuesday could further hamper firefighting efforts.Macron said a smaller fire in the Landes region had been contained, but the fight continued in neighbouring Gironde. While firefighters had made progress on Monday, improving the situation compared to 24 hours before, he warned that "temperatures are set to rise again, the wind is still present, and therefore we must remain humble".Earlier, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez had said the fire "has a life of its own".Jerome Steffe, the mayor of Cestas, a town south of Bordeaux, told the BBC this "will be the fire of the century".He described how 17,000 residents were evacuated from his town during the night when the fire swelled two days ago. So far, he said, the region has seen 42,000 hectares (103,000 acres) of land burned and 240 houses destroyed."In my city the situation is really catastrophic," he added.And although the fire is no longer moving as quickly, he said his teams have "won only a small battle" and emphasised that the risk remains from flying embers or a sudden change in wind direction."We put all our energy into creating protective firebreaks," he explained, but admitted "we are all scared in front of this situation."French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu warned the country "is going through an unprecedented fire season", with 116,085 hectares (286,852 acres) burned and 13,566 fire starts recorded since January.The minister revealed in a post on X that nine out of 10 fires "are human-caused and most arise from carelessness: a cigarette butt, a barbecue, work carried out without precaution".But he also said that not all these fires are accidents and some are deliberately set, adding that since 6 July, 162 arrests have taken place.Wildfires are also burning in several other French regions, including Var and Landes, and also in Haute-Corse on the island of Corsica.Meanwhile, neighbouring Spain on Monday entered its fifth day of a national emergency because of raging wildfires west of the capital Madrid.BBC Verify has been analysing satellite imagery showing the spread of the wildfire west of Madrid, which has now affected more than 27,000 hectares.Satellite images, captured on 24 and 26 July, show how the fire spread over two days after several blazes in the Almorox, Villa del Prado and San Martín de Valdeiglesias areas merged into one large fire.The images show the rapid expansion of the burn scar as the wildfire spread.Local officials have warned that the region faces the "worst fires in its history".Climate change is driving up temperatures around the world, and Europe is the fastest warming continent, heating up twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service.This is causing increased summer heatwaves, greater pressure on Europe's water supply, and more intense wildfires.

schema.headline: Wildfire now nine miles from French city of Bordeaux, mayor warns

title: Carly Simon reveals Parkinson's diagnosis
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Carly Simon was one of the quintessential singer-songwriters of the 1970s and 80sByMusic correspondentThe sin
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Carly Simon was one of the quintessential singer-songwriters of the 1970s and 80sByMusic correspondentThe singer-songwriter Carly Simon says she has been diagnosed with Parkinson's  and is "learning how to live" with the "sometimes frightening" condition.In a statement provided to the BBC, the 83-year-old described the "unpredictable" progress of the disease, saying: "Some days I'm so tired I can't get the day moving at all. On others, it gives me a little more room to move, think, work, and feel like myself."But I have not stopped living, and I have not stopped working," said the singer, best known for songs like You're So Vain, Why, and Coming Around Again.Simon added that she had recently received surgery to remove a cancerous growth on her face that had "affected my appearance".The surgery "made me more self-conscious about being seen in public," she added. "I have always been more critical of my appearance than anyone else could possibly imagine (check out the irony of having written You're So Vain), and this gave my inner critic quite a lot of new material."Parkinson's is a progressive disorder that affects the brain, nervous system, and muscle control. It is the fastest growing neurological condition in the world, with about 153,000 people in the UK living with the condition.Image caption, The singer performed a special one-off concert for BBC Radio 2 in 2010Simon said her problems began with arthritis in both knees and one of her hips. However, her mobility failed to improve after three replacement surgeries."I had trouble standing up from low chairs and deep couches without someone offering me an arm," she said. "Overstuffed furniture became my enemy. Once seated, I could feel as though I had been swallowed by the chair and might remain there permanently, like a guest who had badly overstayed her welcome."Eventually, there were periods when I could not walk without considerable help. My family and I knew that something more was going on. After an extensive evaluation at the Mayo Clinic, I was diagnosed with Parkinson's."The musician has been receiving medication and treatment; but says the condition also comes with episodes of anxiety, depression, and apathy. "The apathy is particularly strange," she observed. "You can find yourself lying there like a starfish drying in the sun, arms pointing in all directions, while nothing inside is telling you to get up, read, watch, write, sing, call someone, or do much of anything at all."That has been one of the hardest things to explain. It is not simply sadness or laziness. It is as though the part of the brain that sends out invitations to participate in life has temporarily misplaced the guest list."New album due in AugustSimon said she had decided to speak about her diagnosis after she received letters, "kindly wondering about my relative silence, asking how I am and what I have been doing."Despite her health condition, the musician recently announced a new album - Comes In Waves - which will be released in August 2026.The first single, Howl, was released last month. It finds the singer consoling a friend who has just been through a break-up."Howl like the wind, roar like the river / Wail like the rain, cry, shout, and shiver," she advises, her tawny, contralto voice instantly recognisable.A press release said the album would see Simon revisiting familiar themes such as "love, memory, family, self-reckoning, and forgiveness, while allowing space for contradiction, ambiguity, and emotional evolution."One of the most recognisable singer-songwriters of the 1970s, Simon was known for her emotionally honest, piano-led pop anthems, and intricate character studies.Among her most beloved songs are the Bond theme Nobody Does It Better and Legend In Your Own Time, a withering portrait of an arrogant man. The latter was something of a dry run for the scathing You're So Vain - written about actor Warren Beatty (and two other men) .In 2003, she auctioned off the subjects' true identity for $50,000 (£38,000) - on the condition that the winner continued to keep the secret.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The star has been sampled by everyone from Janet Jackson to A Tribe Called QuestIn the statement confirming her Parkinson's diagnosis, Simon said she did not consider the condition "a gift or a blessing". "It is neither," she wrote. "It is difficult, frustrating, and sometimes frightening. I am still learning how to live with it and how to accept it without feeling that I have surrendered something essential."I am still writing, singing, imagining, laughing, worrying, remembering, and occasionally getting trapped in an overstuffed chair.She continued: "I am deeply grateful to my children, my family, my friends, my caregivers, and the medical professionals who have helped me through this. Their love and patience have carried me through days when my own reserves were not enough."These days I move more slowly, I lean on others more than I once did, and I have learned to accept that every day will look a little different. "But I am still very much here."

title: Love Island UK crowns winners of 13th series
description: This article contains spoilers for the Love Island final.Julia Majchrzak and Lorenzo Alessi have been crowned the winners of Love Island UK 2026.The p
body: This article contains spoilers for the Love Island final.Julia Majchrzak and Lorenzo Alessi have been crowned the winners of Love Island UK 2026.The pair beat runners-up Jasmine Muller and Kavan Murphy, and Angelista Gunda and Simba Kudyiwa, who came in third, to take home the £50,000 prize.A shocked Julia thanked all those who had voted for them, saying: "I just didn't think coming into Casa [Amor] I'd be stood here." When host Maya Jama asked what they would spend the money on, Julia revealed she wanted Lorenzo, who appeared too stunned to speak, to move in with her after leaving the villa. Talking to Maya ahead of the reveal during the live final, 28-year-old Lorenzo said he had "never met someone who feels so well matched to me" when reflecting on his relationship with Julia. Business owner Lorenzo, who entered the villa on day one, said he felt like he "manifested" meeting Julia, 26, in Casa Amor, the alternate villa where relationships are tested by new arrivals. Julia said she felt an "instant spark" when meeting Lorenzo and described their relationship as "seriously unserious".Fashion business owner Jasmine, 27, said she had been attracted to 21-year-old Kavan's "aura" when speaking to Maya during the final.Viewers were surprised early in the series when Kavan, who was sent in as a bombshell, was revealed to be the brother of day-one contestant Aidan Murphy.Fans said it was reminiscent of popular Prime Video show The Summer I Turned Pretty, which focuses on a love triangle involving two siblings.During the final, Kavan said he "couldn't be luckier" to have been in the villa with his brother and to have met Jasmine. Simba, who turned 25 in the villa, told Maya his first plan with nurse Angelista once they left the show would be to celebrate her 25th birthday, which is on Tuesday. For the first time in the history of the UK series, only three couples were in the final after several shock twists rocked the villa during Sunday's episode.Firstly, ex-islanders returned to vote for the couple they felt should be dumped from the island. After the votes were counted, Mica Harris and Samraj Toor were forced to leave having received the most.Before they left, the pair were tasked with picking one other couple who they felt should also leave.It was revealed at the start of Monday's episode that Yasmin Hadlow and Tommy Stagg were going to miss out on a place in the final. Afterwards, Tommy comforted Yasmin, telling her: "I've got you and that's all I care about." The dating show, which is on its 13th UK series, has tried to keep viewers on their toes over the past eight weeks by bringing in 32 islanders. From the get-go, they changed things up by giving bombshells Yasmin and George Knight the power to dump day-one contestants Ellie Chadwick and Samraj from the villa.However, it was soon revealed they were not actually going home, and were sent on dates with two new bombshells instead. The series also saw islander Priya Jaswal receive some pushback from fellow contestants and viewers after she took a jab at dumped islander Elicia Bailey. After Priya found out Elicia had branded her as the "biggest game player" on Love Island: Aftersun, she said she should "go back" to her job at National Rail instead of appearing on the aftermath show.Kavan responded by saying there's "nothing wrong with working on the National Rail".  RMT Union, which represents rail workers, weighed in on the discussion by resharing the video to their Instagram followed by clips of people working on the train lines, ending with the message: "Rail workers and proud".Priya later apologised for her comment on Aftersun, saying it was "completely out of line" and "catty".She added that her emotions had become "very heightened" after spending weeks in the villa.During the live final, Priya directly apologised to Elicia, and clarified it was "not meant to be a job-shaming comment".

schema.headline: Love Island UK crowns winners of 13th series

title: France and Spain wildfires: Witnesses describe 'wall of flames', fear and stress
description: Chris De Abreu, who is from Kent but works in France and has a flat in Bordeaux, described how "over the weekend the city was engulfed in smoke with t
body: Chris De Abreu, who is from Kent but works in France and has a flat in Bordeaux, described how "over the weekend the city was engulfed in smoke with the sun disappearing behind", with an "orange-like filter" over the city.Though De Abreu said he is less concerned about his flat which lies on the other side of the river, he "can see a number of people worried about what is to come".Elsewhere, Rachel Hanberry told BBC Radio 5 Live that her beachfront home in Biscarrosse Plage, which lies about 63km (40 miles) from Bordeaux, is located next to the town's evacuation point. "Everyone came here on Thursday night," she said. "People had nowhere to go. We offered our home to people."The community there has "lost so much", she added. "The stress and trauma that you feel as someone living here is immense." About 700km away, in Cotignac in the south-east of France, Jo Barnes and her family returned to their home on Saturday, having evacuated for four days after a fire rapidly moved towards their property. "A wall of orange flames came roaring up over the hill," Barnes said. "On Friday afternoon, the fire came back to our area... within 10 metres of the back of our house, we have a gas tank here, it was all very dramatic." Though the surrounding hillside was blackened and charred, the town of Cotignac was undamaged and the Barnes' family home left intact. In the central Madrid region of Spain, where more than 27,000 hectares (66,000 acres) have burnt, residents have faced similar ordeals. "Everyone had to get out of the village quickly, it was a critical situation and people were scared," Olga Congacha told AFP news agency.She and her husband did not take much: "[We] left with all that we could grab, our important documents, some clothes".In the eastern Castellón province, Ricardo Pozo told AFP that he had "never seen a fire this intense before". "I've seen major fires, but on television. Nothing like this, here and now." Maria Garcia, who lives in Betxí - also in the Castellón province - described to Reuters how the fires had put life on pause for those who evacuated: "You can't go out to work, you can't go about your daily life." "You can see the mountains you've known your whole life burning," she added.The wildfires have also upended plans for holidaymakers. James Hillier had been visiting his son in the seaside community of Lacanau about 42 km (26 miles) east of Bordeaux in the Gironde department."The whole town got consumed by smoke," he told the BBC. "There was ash falling from the sky and I noticed a big lump of it landed on my hand."He and his wife left the town for Bordeaux on Saturday, but found that in the city "the air was acrid - it stung your eyes and people were wearing masks". They have since left to go to somewhere in the north of the France instead. Sarah from Hertfordshire realised that her family would have to cut their week-long holiday in Bordeaux short because of the smoke. "We sealed all the apartment up, but it still had a really strong smell of smoke everywhere. It was quite worrying," she said.She then warned her sister-in-law Georgia, whose family had been due to join them in the Bordeaux region in Lacanau, not to come. Georgia booked to stay in another region instead.Georgia said she has not been able to secure a refund from her accommodation operator because the fire had not yet reached Lacanau at the time of cancellation. "If we don't find a solution with them we currently stand to lose over £3,500," Georgia added.

schema.headline: France and Spain wildfires: Witnesses describe 'wall of flames', fear and stress

title: Jack Draper: Long-term arm injury rules former British number one out of Mubadala DC Open
description: The former world number four has only played 14 matches in the past 12 months, largely because of the bruised humerus which he has tried to overcome b
body: The former world number four has only played 14 matches in the past 12 months, largely because of the bruised humerus which he has tried to overcome by resting for long periods."It's hard to tell when you can push [and] when not to push," Draper said at Wimbledon."At the end of the day I'm playing a very aggressive sport, that you need to play through some stuff. Sometimes it's too much. Sometimes it's not."I wouldn't be competing anywhere if there was a chance that I'm going to get a lot worse, for instance."Draper's initial comeback earlier this season was derailed by tendinitis in his knee and the three-time ATP Tour winner had not played for more than two months before his return at Eastbourne in June.Reaching the semi-finals came at a price, though, with his arm injury flaring up again at Wimbledon and leaving Draper "devastated" at having to pull out of his home Grand Slam.Draper, who is now ranked 147th in the world, has not played a major since the US Open in August.If he is fit enough to play at Flushing Meadows this year, he will have to come through qualifying - or be given a wildcard - to play in the main draw.In Washington, Draper will be replaced in the draw by lucky loser Mackenzie McDonald.

schema.headline: Jack Draper: Long-term arm injury rules former British number one out of Mubadala DC Open

title: Badenoch calls for emergency legislation to stop early release scheme
description: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has called for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to bring in emergency legislation in order to stop the early release of h
body: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has called for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to bring in emergency legislation in order to stop the early release of hundreds of prisoners.Burnham announced last week that he was pausing the scheme, which would have seen about 700 prisoners freed in the first phase in September, following a backlash from survivors and victims.But the Conservatives say the government's review will not stop offenders being released. The scheme was part of a bid to stop unprecedented overcrowding, which Labour says was caused by Conservative governments failing to build new prisons.A Labour spokesperson said: "It's this government that is fixing the Tories' mess."Early release was first used by the Conservative government, external in 2023 because of prison overcrowding, first for 18 and then 70 days, and 10,000 prisoners had been released early by June 2024 - before Labour came to power.When Sir Keir Starmer entered Downing Street in July 2024, there were fewer than 100 spare prison places across the adult male estate, which is what prompted the Sentencing Act to release another 6,000 prisoners early from September.While the act already excludes the most serious and dangerous offenders, such as murderers serving life sentences or those on extended sentences, the eligibility for early release is based on the length of sentence, external, rather than the type of offence.Badenoch is calling on Burnham to fast-track legislation to keep serious offenders behind bars."It's all well and good cutting bills and bus fares, but that pales into insignificance when paedophiles and rapists are about to be let out on our streets," she is expected to say at a press conference with victims on Tuesday."Burnham needs to show us he's ready to take the tough decisions."Without emergency legislation, Badenoch says dangerous offenders will start to be released the day after MPs return to Parliament after the summer recess on Tuesday 1 September.She is calling on Burnham to revoke legislation coming into effect on 2 September and if necessary recall Parliament to ensure the worst violent and sexual offenders are exempted from early release.Conservative shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said: "Victims should not have to live in fear all summer waiting for a review."The clock is ticking. Thousands of rapists, paedophiles, and other serious criminals are set to be released in September. "Labour must act now and stop the mass release of dangerous criminals."Earlier this month, the Conservative front bench sought to put pressure on the government to rethink the earlier release plans, saying that it would mean some rapists would leave prison sooner than expected. The government stood by the plan, saying it was a political choice to manage offenders on strict conditions in the community, rather than see the collapse of the system, leaving sex offenders and others to act with impunity.Burnham's decision to pause the scheme came after criticism from the family of Thames Valley Police officer Andrew Harper, who was killed in Berkshire in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road by three teenagers.Two of the killers of PC Harper, who were both sentenced to 13 years in prison, would have benefited from the scheme from June 2027, when the longest fixed sentences would have been added.PC Harper's widow Lissie called the plans "deplorable" and said politicians were "making decisions from behind a desk that will have real and lasting consequences" for the families of victims.Defending the review of the Sentencing Act that has been announced by Burnham, a Labour Party spokesperson said: "The Conservatives have some nerve. "During their 14 years in office, they shut 23 prisons, created just 482 jail places, and granted early release to 10,000 prisoners - leaving the criminal justice system teetering on verge of collapse."It's this government that is fixing the Tories' mess. We have already delivered over 3,000 prison places and we're investing billions to deliver thousands more."Liberal Democrat justice spokesperson Jess Brown-Fuller MP said: "The reality is that in a properly functioning justice system, no victim or loved ones should ever be told that their perpetrator is being released earlier than expected."Unfortunately, the Conservatives left our prisons on the brink of collapse, creating a capacity crisis that required emergency action to keep the system functioning and the public safe."Now that the government claims to have increased prison capacity, there is a clear opportunity for Burnham to correct some of the mistakes made by his predecessors with this scheme."Reform UK's Home Affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf said the "disastrous" policy had been introduced by the Tories, and Badenoch had in 2024 supported efforts to expand it."It's clear that only one party has consistently opposed early release and proposed strong law and order reforms to ensure hardened criminals are locked up for the full duration of their sentences," Yusuf said in a statement."Only Reform UK will fix lawless Britain," the party's Home Affairs spokesperson added.

schema.headline: Badenoch calls for emergency legislation to stop early release scheme

title: English football agrees trial to end goalkeeper tactical timeout
description: English football will implement a trial to try to eradicate the goalkeeper tactical timeout this season.The Football Association, Premier League, Engl
body: English football will implement a trial to try to eradicate the goalkeeper tactical timeout this season.The Football Association, Premier League, English Football League, National League and Women's Super League have agreed on the measure, with permission granted by the International Football Association Board (Ifab).Pro Ref, led by chief refereeing officer Howard Webb, had been in discussions with the leagues to determine how to tackle the issue. It settled on a team having to remove an outfield player from the pitch. If a referee signals that the physio can come on to treat a goalkeeper, that team's coach will have 10 seconds to nominate another player to leave the pitch for one minute after play has restarted, telling the fourth official of their choice.If no player has been selected within 10 seconds, the captain must leave the field.The first game to feature the trial will be the Carabao Cup preliminary round tie between Tranmere and Rochdale on Saturday.BBC Sport understands that the Australian A-League will trial a variation with the captain always having to leave the field.The tactic of gaining a timeout as the keeper is treated has become increasingly common and controversial in recent seasons.It has not been uncommon for the goalkeeper to sit on the turf and signal for the physio, with all the other players rushing to the technical area for a team talk. As soon as the coach has delivered their instructions, the keeper gets up to play on.Goalkeeper treatment has also been used to disrupt the opposition's momentum when they are on top.In November, Leeds United boss Daniel Farke accused Manchester City goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma of feigning injury to "bend the rules" and break up play.Ifab, meanwhile, has issued a clarification to the mistaken identity rule after Fifa used it to book two players for simulation at the World Cup.Paraguay's Miguel Almiron and Breel Embolo of Switzerland both received bookings. Embolo was already on a caution meaning he was sent off in the quarter-final defeat by Argentina.Ifab says that while it was well received and will be included in the detailed review of the VAR protocol, it "may not be used as such until that review is concluded".At Ifab's AGM in February, head of referees Pierluigi Collina said finding a solution to stop the goalkeeper tactical timeout was a priority.At the 2026 World Cup, Collina told his officials to prevent players from going to the technical area on all stoppages.The effectiveness of the measure is open to debate, as the three-minute hydration breaks in each half created a natural opportunity for a team talk.In its own discussions, English football felt that merely stopping players going to the technical area would not deter coaches from using goalkeepers to break up play.English football chose this trial as it follows the logic applied to outfield players, who must themselves leave the field for one minute if the physio comes on.It is intended to be proactive as a deterrent rather than reactive to a team talk as it happens. Match of the Day pundit Danny Murphy suggested last season that lawmakers could act to close the loophole in this exact way."I think they can change it really quickly," Murphy said. "If a keeper goes down injured, instead of him having to go off, one of the outfield players should go off then it's fair all round. "It's a little change that makes a world of difference."Officials will not prevent players from visiting the touchline as an injury is treated but it is hoped the prospect of playing with 10 players for a minute will act as an adequate disincentive.This is especially the case in the final minutes of games, when teams trying to hold on to a result would use the goalkeeper to kill momentum. Now they would have to play with 10 players.There are a few exemptions when a team-mate will not have to go off.Where a goalkeeper says they do not need the physio and they have not caused play to stopThe goalkeeper and an outfield player have collidedIf a goalkeeper is fouled and needs immediate treatmentIf a goalkeeper is bleedingIf there is a serious injury (has to be substituted) or concussion.If the goalkeeper is substituted, the substitution is not delayed.There have been some concerns that a requirement to leave the field for one minute could lead to players, both goalkeepers and outfield, attempting to play on with an injury. The results of the trials will be assessed by Ifab at its meetings throughout the seasons, and this could lead to a permanent law change globally from 2027-28.

schema.headline: English football agrees trial to end goalkeeper tactical timeout

title: Attachment theory explained and how to become secure
description: Why attachment theory is everywhere right now and how it can help youImage source, Lizzy SmithImage caption, Lizzy Smith says she used to see her diff
body: Why attachment theory is everywhere right now and how it can help youImage source, Lizzy SmithImage caption, Lizzy Smith says she used to see her difficulty with relationships as "completely unsolvable"ByJosh ElginFor Lizzy, relationships always seemed to end the same way. "I would get to a second or third date and find something wrong with them." Just as things began to feel real, the connection she longed for would suddenly feel uncomfortable, even threatening. And she would pull away.For years, she couldn't explain why - until she came across attachment theory.And it was the description of a so-called fearful-avoidant - one of the four attachment styles - which felt strikingly familiar.It describes someone who wants closeness, but worries that people in their life will eventually reject or abandon them."It was like I had found the missing piece to a puzzle that I've been trying to solve for years," Lizzy says.She is not alone. Attachment theory has exploded into the public consciousness.On TikTok, videos tagged #AttachmentTheory have racked up hundreds of millions of views.And in popular culture it's used to explain everything from Marianne and Connell's relationship in the hit book and TV series Normal People to the lyrics of Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's record-breaking number one track Rein Me In."The first time I listened to it I started crying," Lizzy says.For her, the song gave voice to both sides of avoidant attachment: the fear that can make love feel unbearable, and the confusion felt by the partner left behind.What are the four attachment styles?First developed in the 1950s by British psychiatrist John Bowlby, attachment theory suggests that the bonds we form with early caregivers shape our expectations of relationships.If support is consistently available, you are more likely to see others as reliable. If care is unpredictable or emotionally distant, you may develop strategies designed to protect yourself from disappointment or distress.There are four attachment styles - anxious, avoidant, fearful-avoidant and secure. In simple terms they are defined as follows:Anxious attachment is often associated with worries about rejection or abandonment. People with this attachment style may seek frequent reassurance from those close to them and struggle with low self-worth. They can be highly attuned to changes in other people's behaviour.People with an avoidant attachment style prioritise their independence and find it difficult to open up emotionally or rely on others. They may subconsciously view intimacy as a threat to their autonomy and withdraw when relationships become too emotionally close.Those with fearful-avoidant attachment (also known as disorganised) want close relationships but often struggle to feel safe in them. They may seek connection one moment and withdraw the next. Someone who is secure is comfortable with both closeness and independence in relationships. They are generally able to trust others, communicate their needs and seek support when they need it.Research suggests that secure people tend to fare better not only in romantic relationships, but across life. They manage stress more effectively, cope better with setbacks like rejection or loss and are better colleagues and managers in the workplace.And what began as a way to understand relationships is increasingly influencing how people navigate them.Across social media, attachment styles are used to reassess friendships, make sense of family tensions or rule out potential partners.And relationship coaches promise to reveal the hidden signs of emotional unavailability in a partner or the ways to heal anxious attachment.The misconceptions around attachment theoryDr Pascal Vrticka, an associate professor of psychology at the University of Essex, has spent nearly two decades studying attachment.He says the theory offers "one of the best explanations" for the differences in how people seek support and connection with others.And while he's glad to see it reach a wider audience, he worries the way it is interpreted can be "outdated, misinformed and, in the worst case, harmful.""I think one problem is that people are overgeneralising it and using it in contexts where it might not be the best framework to explain our behaviour," he says.Part of the issue, he explains, is that initial assumptions around attachment theory have evolved since it was first developed.Vrticka says one of the biggest misconceptions is that attachment styles are fixed.Although studies have found that they can show a degree of stability over time, Vrticka says change is possible."The good news is that the evidence shows that secure attachment is the most stable. Which means that once you become secure, you tend to stay secure."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Sam Fender and Olivia Dean accept the BRIT Award for song of the year for Rein Me In, which has been dubbed an "avoidant anthem."He says attachment is often reshaped during periods of transition, particularly during adolescence, when young people begin forming close relationships beyond their family.Later events in our lives, like entering a new relationship, experiencing a breakup or dealing with bereavement, can also be influential.But Vrticka says that change is gradual and professional support is likely to be needed for people with more entrenched attachment patterns.It's that nuance, Lizzy says, which is often lost in discussions of attachment theory.She says some people can be "quick to assume the worst" and reduce others to labels. However, while she says people with insecure attachment styles should be viewed with more empathy, she acknowledges the importance of self-awareness. "For me, I know that my avoidant tendencies are toxic and it would be unfair for me to date someone right now," she says.But, she adds, that doesn't mean people with insecure attachments are incapable of healthy relationships. "It is on you to acknowledge it and put in the work to heal."How do you become secure?Few have played a more influential role in bringing attachment to the mainstream than Dr Amir Levine.His book Attached, co-written with Rachel Heller, was first published in 2010 and has since sold millions of copies around the world.But in his latest book, Levine shifts the focus from identifying attachment styles to ask a different question: how do you become secure?Part of the answer, he argues, lies in what he calls "SIMIs" - seemingly insignificant minor interactions.A text from a friend asking about your weekend. A smile from a stranger."The brain monitors small interactions all the time," Levine says. "That's what attachment is about. It's a monitoring system for safety."And he says these interactions gradually shape what the brain expects from relationships.Positive experiences build evidence that people can be trusted and relied upon, helping move someone towards what he calls "secure mode".Image source, Shira H. WeissImage caption, After helping millions identify their attachment style, Amir Levine is now focused on how those patterns can changeBut equally, a delayed response or a friend failing to follow through on plans can trigger subtle stress responses in the nervous system.Importantly, Levine says it's possible to have different attachment styles with different people.So he encourages people to identify the relationships in their lives that already make them feel safe and understood, and to use them "as a vehicle for becoming more secure overall".And the idea that security can be built through current relationships reflects a broader shift away from seeing attachment as just the result of childhood experiences.For some, discovering attachment theory can involve re-examining family relationships, which can potentially lead to resentment. But Levine says "it's not just about where you started, but what happens afterwards"."If that way of thinking helps you understand yourself and move forward, that's useful," he says."But if it makes you feel stuck or damaged, then it's not accurate because people really can change."Levine also argues that insecure attachments can in themselves be strengths.Complex with Kimberley WilsonWhat is anxious attachment?He says anxious people are often acutely tuned into relationships, spotting subtle shifts in mood, tone and behaviour that others miss, while avoidant people can be fiercely independent and perform well under pressure.However, whilst Vrticka agrees that attachment styles shouldn't be seen as either good or bad, he stresses they "come with certain risks and difficulties", which he says shouldn't be disregarded.But both agree that attachment theory is most useful when it helps people understand patterns rather than define themselves.

schema.headline: Attachment theory explained and how to become secure

title: China's new challenge as natural disasters strike - fake AI videos
description: As China deals with the fallout of Typhoon Noul that made landfall over the weekend, officials will be painfully aware that they will likely have an a
body: As China deals with the fallout of Typhoon Noul that made landfall over the weekend, officials will be painfully aware that they will likely have an additional challenge to deal with: dangerously misleading videos created with Artificial Intelligence (AI).Powerful storms and flooding incidents over the last few months have seen fake videos inundating social media platforms –  these include images of dead bodies floating in floodwaters, the false depiction of severe flooding in areas actually not affected and others with blatantly fake details of emergency response efforts.In some areas, videos containing false information about power outages prompted residents to panic buy emergency supplies.Other videos capitalise on real-life incidents. Flooding in Hengzhou city, Guangxi in early July caused hundreds of snakes to escape from a breeding farm. Then fake images were also published showing crocodiles being released into a river.In an already tense and dangerous situation involving mass evacuations and complex rescue operations, authorities want to avoid panic. Now they fear that AI technology - which China is pouring billions of dollars into - is providing simple, accessible tools that can be used to trick the public."Many of these content creators use disaster news to try to gain followers, knowing that more sensational or exaggerated content will garner more likes and more views. They are deliberately fabricating information to grab people's attention," Huang Zhihua, Deputy Chief in charge of online public security for Zhejiang Police Department told Chinese state media.In recent weeks, there have been arrests and punishment – ranging from detention awaiting criminal prosecution to fines – for the creation of bogus reports and video content.But experts are warning that an unprecedented crisis of misinformation could be looming.In an article published by the newspaper of the Communist Party's Central Party School, Professor Chen Bin said, "AI dramatically lowers the technical barriers to producing false information. Individuals no longer require sophisticated technical skills. By simply prompting AI tools, they can rapidly generate convincing text, images, audio and video… which is highly realistic but entirely fabricated content, manufactured on a large scale."Professor Gao Fuping, from the East China University of Political Science and Law, told the BBC that motivation for the publishing of such false content ranges from those who do it "to create something amusing without thinking about the consequences", to those who want to "generate traffic for personal gain" or those who wish to deliberately "cause panic or social unrest"."Some users think the online world is anonymous and unregulated or that they cannot be traced," he said.There have been calls for all AI-generated content to be clearly stamped but other users can then just re-edit the material removing the markings.Professor Xu Xiaoke from Beijing Normal University told the BBC that greater efforts were also needed to verify geographic locations with timestamps and the checking of image sources."That said, I would also stress that detection technology still lags behind generation technology. We're in a constant cat-and-mouse game. So we should not assume that technology alone can identify AI-generated content with the click of a button," he warned.The Chinese government is embracing AI in its bid to become the leading tech superpower.In 2017,  it announced that AI would be "the main driving force" of the country's progress.Vast sums of money is pouring into AI businesses seeking more capital, fuelling domestic competition. The state-controlled wire service Xinhua reports that the country has over 6,000 "AI companies".In this climate,  Prof Xu believes that China needs to build "trusted information infrastructure". This could include official government early warning systems and disaster interfaces which news organisations can access.But there have been instances of official sources, including government-controlled media, deliberately downplaying disasters, which has led to some public mistrust in this area.Earlier in July, local journalists were asked to "soften" their language to describe a major breach in the wall of the Liulan Dam near Naning as an "opening" or "gap".Officials appeared to be trying to make the breach sound less alarming but the consequences were deadly.  Water bursting through the broken dam led to at least 26 deaths downstream.And this is not an isolated incident.In 2021, local officials were arrested, accused of concealing or underreporting 139 deaths in Henan province.Incidents like these have resulted in a trust vacuum that has made it much easier for bad actors to spread fake content.But police are imploring people to trust accredited sources during emergencies."When encountering disaster-related information from an unknown source, approach it with scepticism and rely on official announcements," Gao Kai from the Ningbo Public Security Bureau said.He also tried to reassure the public that the creators of false information would be caught, saying that "the internet is not a lawless zone. Public security authorities will continue to intensify efforts to crack down on illegal online activity"."We've created a specialised task force to monitor social media closely, especially short video platforms. They will investigate and handle these cases quickly, cracking down in a very strict manner".Punishment could range from a fine to up to seven years in prison if the fallout of the misinformation is serious enough.On 23 July, China's Cyberspace Administration also announced a nationwide crackdown on fake internet content related to floods and other disasters, ordering its local branches to focus on catching out fabricated data, malicious editing, staged scenes, misattributed historical events and those impersonating officials. In addition, it called on social media platforms to strengthen the review of the content they are publishing.Prof Gao believes "the answer is public education combined with law enforcement", saying that there was a "need to publicise real cases where people have been punished."He added that "the harm caused by AI-generated fake content is ultimately the result of how people choose to use the technology - not the technology itself", adding that existing laws were sufficient to deal with it.However, others are not so confident.  Professor Chen pointed out that "AI technology continues to evolve much faster than legal frameworks. As new legal questions emerge, AI misinformation remains a considerable challenge."Shanghai and Washington based lawyer Peter Pang says lawyers around the world are seeing an explosion in the number of cases dealing with these issues.He believes that the companies that create AI apps and the platforms used to publish fake videos and other material must be held legally accountable along with the people who create misinformation."The first line would be the platforms, because they're the ones that are the enablers. They're the ones that allow this to go out," he told the BBC.He used a hypothetical example of a person who runs over a pedestrian following panic induced by a fake post on social media."The video creator might say 'you ran over somebody. That's your problem. I didn't do it.' But let's think it through. You created the foundation from which people reacted. If you created that panic, you need to have responsibility for consequences that occur."And Professor Xu warns that "AI-generated misinformation is likely to increase not only in volume but in the speed with which it spreads.""Looking ahead, political elections, public health emergencies, armed conflicts, natural disasters and issues affecting people's livelihoods are all likely to become high-risk areas for AI-generated misinformation."Instead of waiting for false information to go viral before trying to contain it, governments and platforms should now be preparing in advance."

schema.headline: China's new challenge as natural disasters strike - fake AI videos
